title: Common patterns: two pointers, sliding window, counting
summary: Three patterns that solve a large share of array and string questions, the signal words that tell you which one to reach for, and the conditions under which each one breaks.
youWillLearn: How to spot a pattern from the signal words in a problem
Frequency counting with a Map: duplicates, anagrams, most common
Two pointers on sorted data: pairs in O(n) without extra memory
Sliding window for contiguous runs, fixed and variable size, and when it fails

glossary.pattern: A reusable shape of solution that fits a whole family of problems, like a design pattern for code.
glossary.frequency count: A Map from each value to how many times it appears, built in one pass.
glossary.anagram: A word made from exactly the same letters as another, in a different order, like "listen" and "silent".
glossary.two pointers: Two index variables that move through an array, often from both ends toward the middle, to avoid checking every pair.
glossary.sliding window: A start and end index marking a stretch of neighboring items. The window slides forward instead of being rebuilt each time.
glossary.contiguous: Next to each other with no gaps, like characters 3 to 7 of a string, as opposed to any picks from anywhere.

steps.title: Two hundred problems, still lost on the next
body: A common way to prepare: solve hundreds of problems and hope the interview repeats one. Then the interviewer changes a detail, and the memorized answer no longer fits.
The way out is to notice that most array and string problems are variations on a few patterns. Learn to recognize the pattern, and a new problem becomes a familiar one.

callout.text: Like UI patterns. You do not memorize every settings page ever made. You recognize "this is a list with detail" or "this is a wizard" and reach for the right structure.

scene.caption: Every problem looks new, until you see which pattern it is.

steps.title: Read the signal words
body: Problems drop hints. "How many", "most common", "duplicate", "anagram": count things. "Sorted" plus "pair" or "two items": two pointers. "Subarray", "substring", "in a row", "longest stretch": sliding window.
Say the match out loud in the interview: "This asks for a contiguous stretch, so I'm thinking sliding window." It shows the structure of your thinking before any code.

scene.caption: Signal words on the left point to a pattern on the right.

steps.title: Frequency counting: tally in one pass
body: Walk the input once and keep a frequency count in a Map: value to how many times you saw it. You met the Map in lesson 3; this is its most common job.
Then answer from the counts: the most common tag, any duplicates, or whether two words are an anagram (same letters, same counts). O(n) time, O(k) space, where k is the number of distinct values.

code.caption: Sorting both strings also works, but costs O(n log n).

scene.caption: "Most common", "duplicate", "anagram": build a tally, then read it.

steps.title: Two pointers: squeeze from both ends
body: Notely's summary budget is 1,000 tokens, and note sizes are sorted. Find two notes that fill it exactly. Lesson 3 solved this with a Map. Sorted data allows two pointers, which need no extra memory.
Put one pointer at the smallest note, one at the largest, and add them. 100 + 750 = 850: too small. Only moving the left pointer up can make the sum bigger.

scene.caption: Smallest plus largest is under budget, so the left pointer must move right.

steps.title: Each move rules out a whole row of pairs
body: Move left to 250: 250 + 750 = 1,000. Found. If a sum is too big, move the right pointer down instead.
Why is skipping safe? When 100 + 750 was too small, 100 plus anything smaller than 750 is too small as well, so 100 can be dropped entirely. Each step removes one item: O(n) time, O(1) space.

code.caption: Only works because sizes is sorted. On unsorted data, sort first or use the Map.

scene.caption: The left pointer glides to 250. Together with 750, that is exactly 1,000.

steps.title: Sliding window: slide, don't rebuild
body: New question: which three contiguous messages in Maya's chat used the most tokens? Adding up every group of three from scratch repeats work.
A sliding window keeps a running sum. To slide one step, add the item entering on the right and subtract the one leaving on the left. Every item enters once and leaves once: O(n).

callout.text: You will meet windows again in AI apps: splitting a long document into overlapping chunks before creating embeddings is a window sliding over the text. And the sliding-window rate limiter from system design is the same idea, sliding over time.

scene.caption: The window slides one step: +800 enters, −200 leaves. 2,000 is the busiest run.

steps.title: Variable windows: grow right, shrink left
body: Some windows change size. Classic: the longest stretch of a string with no repeated character. Grow the window to the right. When the new character is already inside, move the left edge just past its last position.
A Map of "last seen index" makes the jump O(1). Two indexes that only move forward: O(n).

code.caption: Patterns combine: a sliding window that uses a Map.

scene.caption: The second "a" pushes the left edge past the first one. Window: b, c, a, d.

steps.title: Every pattern has a precondition
body: Patterns fail quietly when their condition is missing. Two pointers needs sorted data; sorting first adds O(n log n). A shrinking window for "smallest stretch with sum at least X" needs no negative numbers: with negatives, shrinking can raise the sum, and the logic breaks.
Before using a pattern, say its precondition out loud and check it against the input.

callout.text: Ask Claude Code to name the pattern it used and its precondition: "Does this assume sorted input? Non-negative values?" Then ask for a test that breaks the precondition. In practice, ask it for the signal words in a problem, not the solution.

scene.caption: One negative number, and the shrinking-window logic is no longer safe.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Read the signal words. Counting words: a frequency Map. Sorted plus a pair: two pointers from both ends. Contiguous stretch: a sliding window that adds on the right and drops on the left.
Each turns O(n²) into O(n), and each has a precondition. Name it before you code.

scene.caption: Three patterns, three signals, three preconditions.

quiz.question: "Given Maya's daily word counts, find the 7-day stretch with the highest total." Which pattern fits best?

options.why: Two pointers fits pairs in sorted data. Here the days are in time order and you need a contiguous run, not a pair.
"Stretch" signals contiguous days. Keep a running sum: add the new day, subtract the day that leaves. O(n).

options.text: A frequency count of the word counts
options.why: Counting how often each number appears says nothing about which days are next to each other.

quiz.question: Claude Code uses two pointers from both ends to find two note sizes that sum to a budget, but the input comes straight from the database with no order by. What is the risk?

options.text: Moving a pointer only makes sense when the array is sorted, so it can skip the real pair and return null.
options.why: The skip logic relies on sorted order. Add order by size, sort first, or use the Map approach from lesson 3.

options.text: It will be O(n²) instead of O(n).
options.why: The loop still runs in O(n). The problem is not speed, it is silently wrong answers.

options.text: None. Postgres always returns rows in insert order.
options.why: Without order by, Postgres makes no promise about row order.

quiz.question: Which problem is a frequency-count problem?

options.text: Find the longest run of notes written on consecutive days.
options.why: "Longest run" of consecutive items is a sliding window signal.

options.text: In a sorted list of prices, find two that add up to 100.
options.why: Sorted plus pair is the two-pointer signal.

options.text: Check whether two tag names use exactly the same letters.
options.why: Same letters, same counts: tally the letters of one, subtract the other, check nothing goes negative.

takeaways: Read the signal words first: count, sorted pair, or contiguous stretch.
Frequency count: one pass into a Map, then answer from the tallies.
Two pointers: start at both ends of sorted data and move the side that fixes the sum. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Sliding window: add the item entering, drop the item leaving. Never re-add the whole window.
Every pattern has a precondition (sorted, contiguous, non-negative). Say it out loud before you code.
